History has a haunting, intimate way of coming full circle. As a young gay man coming of age, Harvey Milk was my north star—a beacon of courage, authenticity, and hope in a world that routinely demanded our silence. Decades later, life brought me face-to-face with the tragedy that shattered our community, but in the most unexpected and surreal way possible: in 1985, working as a mortician, I found myself preparing the body of Milk’s assassin, Dan White, for burial following his suicide. 

To understand the weight of that quiet moment in the prep room, one must remember the violent storm Dan White unleashed upon San Francisco. White was a conservative ex-cop and ex-fireman who had been elected to the San Francisco Board of Supervisors on the very same day as Harvey Milk in 1977. Despite their shared entry into city politics, the two men represented vastly different visions for the future. Tensions mounted until November 27, 1978, when White snuck through a basement window of City Hall to bypass metal detectors. He brutally assassinated Mayor George Moscone before walking down the hall to execute Harvey Milk, shooting him twice in the head at point-blank range.

The tragedy of the assassinations was compounded by the gross legal injustice that followed. During his trial, White’s defense successfully argued diminished capacity—a strategy infamously dubbed the "Twinkie Defense." Rather than a conviction for cold-blooded, premeditated murder, White was found guilty of the lesser charge of voluntary manslaughter. He was sentenced to a mere seven years in prison and ultimately served only five. 

This shockingly light sentence, along with the immediate public fallout, tore open the city’s wounds and laid bare the deep-seated homophobia woven into the fabric of the justice system. The reality was undeniable: a jury of his peers, influenced by a law enforcement culture where some officers openly sympathized with White, had devalued Harvey Milk’s life simply because he was a gay man. The verdict proved that to the establishment, the murder of a gay trailblazer was not worth a lifetime in prison.

When White was released in 1984, he returned to a city that could neither forgive nor forget his crimes. Unable to escape the guilt and the inescapable shadow of his deeds, he took his own life in a garage in October 1985. Standing over his lifeless body a few days later, preparing him for his final resting place, I felt the heavy, complex irony of my position. Here was the man who had tried to extinguish the voice of a generation, now silent, cold, and entirely helpless beneath the hands of a man who had loved his victim.

In the end, Dan White’s violent act failed in its ultimate purpose. While White died in ignominy, remembered only as a tragic footnote of hatred and despair, Harvey Milk’s voice was never truly silenced. In the decades since his death, Milk has emerged as an enduring, legendary figure whose vision of hope continues to inspire civil rights movements around the globe. Time has rendered its final verdict: the assassin faded into the dark, but Harvey Milk became immortal.

The air in a mortuary prep room is always cold, sterile, and heavy with the sharp, medicinal sting of formaldehyde. It is a space designed for silence and detachment, a boundary zone where the living perform their final duties for the dead. But on an autumn day in October 1985, that professional detachment collapsed under the weight of history when the body on my stainless-steel table was identified as Dan White.

Seven years earlier, on November 27, 1978, White had snuck through a basement window of San Francisco City Hall carrying a .38-caliber revolver. He systematically executed Mayor George Moscone and Supervisor Harvey Milk, California’s first openly gay elected official and a beacon of hope for a marginalized community fighting for its right to exist. 

For the queer community, Milk’s assassination was a devastating blow, but what followed in the courtroom was a secondary trauma—a stark, humiliating lesson in how the American legal system valued gay lives. During the trial, White’s defense team argued that his capacity was diminished, famously citing his sudden shift from a health-conscious lifestyle to consuming junk food—a legal strategy mockingly immortalized as the "Twinkie Defense." More insidiously, the defense leveraged the deep-seated, systemic homophobia of the era, portraying White as a traditional, God-fearing family man pushed to a breaking point by the social changes Milk represented. 

The jury, purged of queer individuals, bought the narrative. Instead of first-degree murder, White was convicted of voluntary manslaughter and sentenced to a mere seven years. He served less than five. The verdict sparked the White Night Riots, a desperate, fiery eruption of grief and rage in the streets of San Francisco. The message from the justice system was undeniable: to destroy a queer champion was a minor offense, easily forgiven by a society that secretly preferred us silenced.

White eventually walked free, but he could not outrun the wreckage of his own mind. In October 1985, unable to find peace or redemption, he attached a hose to his car's exhaust pipe in his wife’s garage, ending his own life. And through a twist of fate that felt almost too heavy to bear, his body was brought to the funeral home where I worked. 

As a queer person, standing over the lifeless form of Dan White was a surreal, harrowing experience. Here was the man whose hate had torn through our community, the man who had tried to erase our rising voice, now completely helpless, motionless, and mute. 

My job was to wash him, embalm him, stitch his incisions, and prepare his body so that his grieving family could look upon him one last time. Every instinct of human anger urged me to turn away, to reject the task. But professionalism—and something deeper—kept my hands steady. 

As I worked, massaging the embalming fluid through his pale limbs to restore a semblance of life to his cold flesh, I felt a quiet, profound irony settling over the room. Systemic homophobia had protected Dan White in life, granting him a leniency he never granted Harvey Milk. Yet in death, the ultimate, unavoidable vulnerability of his physical body required the care of the very people he had hated. 

I dressed him. I applied cosmetics to mask the subtle discoloration left by carbon monoxide poisoning. I set his features into a neutral, peaceful expression. I gave him a dignity in death that he had denied to Harvey, and that his sympathizers in the courts had denied to us. 

There was no grand vengeance in that room, only a quiet, melancholy truth. Dan White died defeated, swallowed by the shadow of his own terrible legacy. Harvey Milk, despite the bullets that took his life, lived on as an immortal symbol of courage, pride, and hope. And as I closed the prep room door behind me, leaving the finished body of Dan White in the dim light, I realized that the ultimate triumph belonged to our community. We were still here—living, working, loving, and even in the darkest rooms, bringing a gentle decency to a world that had so often denied it to us.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, poignant creative writing piece about a gay man in San Francisco who came of age during Harvey Milk's era and ended up preparing Dan White's body for his funeral after White's suicide.
counterfactuals.output:
The autumn of 1985 smelled of cold rain and formaldehyde. In San Francisco, death was no longer a rare visitor; it was a permanent tenant. Julian, at thirty-one, possessed the hands of an old man—calloused, gentle, and perpetually stained with the faint, sweet chemical scent of the mortuary basement. 

In those dark days, Julian spent his mornings preparing the boys from the Castro. Friends, lovers, strangers who had danced under the disco balls at the Elephant Walk just a few summers ago, now reduced to hollow cheeks and sunken eyes by the quiet plague wiping out his generation. Julian dressed them in their silk shirts and leather jackets, combing their hair back so they looked like the vibrant creatures they had been.

So when the gurney rolled into the prep room on a Tuesday afternoon, veiled in heavy black plastic, Julian expected another boy from the neighborhood. 

Then he pulled back the sheet.

The face staring up at the fluorescent lights was not a boy’s. It was broad, square-jawed, and unnaturally flush—a grim side effect of carbon monoxide poisoning. The skin had a strange, cherry-pink hue. 

It was Dan White. 

Julian’s breath hitched, caught in the back of his throat like ash. His mind fractured, tumbling back seven years. 

He was twenty-four again, standing on Castro Street in the blinding sun of 1978. He remembered the sound of Harvey’s voice crackling through a megaphone, loud and brassy and full of impossible, terrifying hope. *“My name is Harvey Milk, and I’m here to recruit you.”* Julian remembered how it felt to be seen for the first time, to walk hand-in-hand down Market Street, believing the world was finally tilting toward grace. 

And then came November 27th. The silence that fell over the city. The hundred thousand candles glowing in the rain. The rage that burned down City Hall when a jury decided that a former cop’s unhappiness, aided by sugar and junk food, was worth more than Harvey’s life, more than Mayor Moscone’s life.

Dan White had served five years. He had come home to the city he broke, retreated into a yellow Buick in his brother’s garage, and run a garden hose from the exhaust pipe into the window. 

Now, he lay on Julian’s stainless-steel table. The murderer and the mourner, alone in a quiet room beneath the city.

Julian’s hands trembled. Every instinct in his body screamed at him to step away, to strip off his rubber gloves, to leave this man to the dark. He thought of Harvey’s bright, toothy smile, reduced to a ghost by the man lying on this cold slab. He felt a wave of hot, ancient fury surge up from his stomach to his throat. 

*Why me?* he thought, looking up at the gray concrete ceiling. *Of all the mortuaries in the city, why did he end up under my hands?*

He stood there for five minutes, maybe ten, listening to the hum of the ventilation fan and the distant rumble of the N-Judah streetcar passing above. 

Slowly, Julian reached into the metal sink and turned on the tap. He worked the soap into a lather between his palms. 

He did not do it out of forgiveness. Forgiveness was a holy, heavy thing, and Dan White had left no room for it in San Francisco. Julian did it because death was a terrible equalizer, and to deny this body dignity would be to let Dan White corrupt him, too. Harvey had taught them about humanity—about standing tall, even when the world wanted you in the dark.

Julian took a soft sponge, dipped it in warm water, and gently wiped the carbon dust from Dan White’s forehead. 

He washed the quiet, folded hands that had once held a .38 Chief’s Special. He worked carefully around the neck, shaving the stubborn stubble along the jawline with a steady, practiced stroke. He closed the pale, vacant eyes, pressing the eyelids down until they stayed. 

When it came time to dress him, Julian pulled a clean white shirt over the dead man's shoulders. As he buttoned the collar, Julian leaned in close, his nose inches from the ear of the man who had tried to break his world.

"Harvey is still everywhere," Julian whispered, his voice barely a breath against the cold air of the room. "We are still here."

Julian turned off the overhead light, leaving the body in the dim, amber glow of the exit sign. He walked out into the San Francisco night, pulled his coat tight against the bay fog, and walked toward the Castro, where the streetlights were burning bright.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a prose poem exploring the aftermath of the Milk-Moscone assassinations from the unique vantage point of the undertaker who made Dan White presentable for burial.
counterfactuals.output:
Carbon monoxide leaves a deceptive pink upon the cheek, a mock-bloom of life that feels like an insult to the dead. It was my task to tone it down, to turn that unnatural, asphyxiated flush back into the dull, respectable pallor of a proper Irish-Catholic funeral. 

Seven years after the shots echoed through the marble corridors of City Hall, Dan White finally came to my table. The city outside my brass-handled doors was still soaked in fog and lingering grief, still fluttering with rainbow flags snapped at half-mast in the mind’s eye, but inside, there was only the smell of formaldehyde and the heavy, cold geometry of a body that had exhausted its own shame. 

I washed his hands first. They were broad, calloused, unremarkable hands—hands that had once pinned on a firefighter’s badge, held a police revolver, and later, pulled the choke on a garden hose in a closed garage. I worked the mortuary cream into his knuckles, smoothing the dry skin, wondering if violence leaves a chemical residue that a soap solution can’t lift. 

How do you make a monster presentable to his mother, his widow, his sons? You do it by remembering that on the embalming table, history is stripped away, leaving only gray muscle and stubborn bone. I brushed powder across the hard jaw that had once clenched through the trials, the riots, the light sentence that felt like a second murder to the streets of the Castro. I used a fine curve of suture wire to tie his lips into a neutral, silent line—stitching shut the mouth that had never found a way to say *forgive me*, sealing it against the ghost of Harvey’s bullhorn and Moscone’s gentle greeting. 

I combed his dark hair, parting it on the left, the way he wore it when he was just a clean-cut boy from the district, before the dark suit and the hollowed eyes. I dressed him in a dark jacket—simple, understated. I tucked a white handkerchief into his pocket, smoothing the linen with a gloved thumb. 

When I was finished, he looked asleep, harmless, as if he had never splintered the heart of San Francisco with five quick squeezes of a trigger. But as I leaned down to check the seal on the casket, the quiet in the room grew suffocating. You can turn a man into a peaceful statue for an hour in a chapel, but you cannot cosmetize a tragedy. I turned off the overhead lights, leaving him in the soft, warm glow of the velvet-draped parlor, knowing that no matter how seamless my work, the lid would never truly close on what he’d done. Outside, the Pacific wind blew down the avenues, cold and unappeased, washing the city in a rain that refused to clean the stain away.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: "I was twenty and living in the Castro when Harvey Milk was killed. In 1985, as a mortician, I prepared Dan White's body for burial." Write a lyrical monologue based on this setup.
counterfactuals.output:
I was twenty then, and the Castro was a city made of glass and velvet. We thought we were unkillable. We walked down Eighteenth Street in the sun like we’d invented sunlight ourselves, loud and beautiful and reckless with our own breath. And Harvey—Harvey was the mayor of our bright, desperate little republic. He had a voice like a brass horn and a smile that looked like a window thrown open in a room that had been locked for fifty years. 

When they shot him in November, the warmth went out of the pavement. I remember the candle wax dripping onto my boots as ten thousand of us marched down Market Street in a silence so deep you could hear the flames licking the air. We carried our grief like a lit fuse.

Seven years pass faster than a tide turning in the Bay. By nineteen eighty-five, I had traded my leather jacket for a dark suit and a pair of latex gloves. I became a mortician. In those days, in San Francisco, if you were young and you knew how to handle the dead, you were never out of work. The city was filling up with shadows, and someone had to wash them, dress them, and lay them down softly. I learned the geography of cold skin. I learned how to close an eye that didn’t want to stay shut.

And then, on an October morning, they wheeled him in.

Dan White.

He had choked himself on carbon monoxide in a garden hose and a Buick, out in the Sunset. Suicide. The news anchor called it a tragedy; the streets called it a long-overdue accounting. But on my table, he was just six feet of heavy, graying meat, smelling of exhaust and damp garage floor.

I stood over him under the humming fluorescent lights. Just me, the stainless steel, and the man who had torn the heart out of my youth.

My hands trembled inside the plastic gloves. I thought of the five bullets. I thought of Harvey lying on the parquet floor of City Hall, his blood sinking into the wood. I thought of the Twinkie defense, the five-year sentence, the riots, the night the police cars burned like dry pine. I had the power then. I had the soap, the trocars, the thick twine, the scalpels. I could have left him twisted. I could have made his mouth look bitter. I could have etched our vengeance into his cold cheekbones.

But death is a strange church, and the prep room is its altar.

I turned on the water. It ran lukewarm and clear.

I washed his face. I washed the grease from his silver hair. I took his hands—the heavy, blunt hands of a cop and a fireman, the hands that held the .38 Special—and I scrubbed the black engine soot from beneath his fingernails. They were calloused, ordinary hands. They felt no different than the hands of the young boys I’d buried the week before, thin as dried leaves, taken by the plague.

That was the cruelest revelation of all: that evil has no special texture. It rots just like innocence. It cools to the same dull marble.

I set his jaw. I applied the arterial fluid, watching the gray flush leave his cheeks, replaced by that false, pink illusion of sleep we sell to the living. I parted his hair on the left, the way he wore it in his supervisor portraits. I put him in a dark blue suit.

I didn't forgive him. Forgiveness is for the living, and Harvey was still dead. The Castro was still full of ghosts. But I gave him grace. Not for his sake, but for ours. Because if I had butchered his memory on that table, if I had let hate guide my scalpel, I would have given him the last piece of my soul, too.

When I was finished, I stepped back. He looked quiet. He looked small. A failed man in a neat suit, waiting for the earth.

I leaned down close to his ear—close enough to smell the faint, sweet perfume of the embalming powder—and I whispered to him, soft as a candle flickering in the fog:

*"Harvey says hello."*

Then I pulled the sheet over his face, turned off the lights, and stepped out into the San Francisco sun.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a historical flash fiction piece about the legacy of Dan White and Harvey Milk, contrasting the 1978 Castro Street community with Dan White's 1985 suicide, ending with the line: "And he was made presentable by a queer."
counterfactuals.output:
In November of 1978, Castro Street smelled of fresh paint, rain-slicked asphalt, and an incandescent, impossible hope. Outside Castro Camera, Harvey Milk stood with his sleeves rolled up, a bullhorn slung over his shoulder, his laughter catching the crisp autumn air. Above him, the newly raised rainbow flags snapped in the Pacific breeze. The street was a sanctuary carved from decades of shame—a place where young men walked hand in hand under Victorian eaves, believing, for the very first time, that the future belonged to them. 

Across town, Dan White sat in the shadows of City Hall, feeling the world he understood curdle beneath his feet. A former cop, a former firefighter, a man of tight collars and unyielding grievances, White viewed the changing city not as a dawn, but as a siege. When he slipped through a basement window with a .38 revolver, he believed he was firing a shot for order. He thought killing Harvey Milk would put out the light. 

Instead, the light multiplied. That night, thirty thousand people marched down Market Street in absolute, candlelit silence—a river of flame that no gun could extinguish. 

Seven years later, the light was still burning on Castro Street, but Dan White was reduced to ash. Released after serving barely five years for voluntary manslaughter—his defense painted in the soft colors of depression and junk food—he returned to San Francisco a pariah, haunted by the ghost of the man he had tried to erase. In October of 1985, in a damp garage in the Sunset District, White taped a hose to the exhaust pipe of his yellow Buick, turned on the radio to a tape of Irish ballads, and let the dark come for him.

The mortuary prep room was cool and quiet, smelling of formaldehyde and iron. The embalmer moved with practiced, gentle hands. He smoothed the dark lapels of the suit, washed the lingering soot from the sunken cheeks, and combed the thinning hair back from the cold forehead. Seven years earlier, this same young man had wept on the steps of City Hall, holding a flickering taper in the November wind. 

Now, he carefully adjusted the knot of the necktie, wiping away the last trace of a bitter life, bestowing a dignity the deceased had spent his final days denying others. 

And he was made presentable by a queer.
